edits.before: A data-processing job can perform the same logical operation under different resource settings. For example, a group-by may run with one worker or two workers, with different thread counts and memory caps. Increasing resources may shorten execution, but it may also increase configured resource-time. Reducing memory can expose pressure, spill or worker restarts. The useful configuration therefore depends on the workload, the deadline and the resource preference.
edits.after: SAFE-Pipe asks a practical question: which resource settings should be used for a supported data-processing job with a specified deadline? The original experiment compares one or two workers, one or two threads per worker, and memory caps of 1 GB or 2 GB per worker [7]. More resources may reduce runtime, but the advisor also accounts for configured resource-time. Dask can spill data or restart workers under memory pressure [6], so the choice cannot be reduced to the number of workers alone.
edits.reason: Replace generic motivation with the actual grid and cite the memory-management claim.

edits.before: The implemented objectives are to collect a reproducible local benchmark table; predict successful engine runtime from pre-run features; add a cautious upper estimate; compare supported configurations under a deadline; explain eligibility and selection; and retain auditable software and experimental records. A later research objective investigated the additional information and cost of execution-based probes.
edits.after: The implemented workflow has three stages: collect measured runtimes for the declared grid, fit and calibrate a runtime predictor, and use the saved artifacts to compare configurations under an engine deadline. Each recommendation includes estimates and eligibility reasons. The later research study asks a separate question: whether executing a small sample supplies useful pressure information at an acceptable profiling cost [7].
edits.reason: Explain the project sequence and separate the research question.

edits.before: The original project title describes a broader failure-aware vision. The implemented evidence is narrower: all original 96 runs succeeded, so those records do not support learning a failure classifier. Later research contains pressure and termination observations, but has not established a calibrated failure model or a beneficial deployed probing policy.
edits.after: The failure-aware objective in the project title remains only partly addressed. All 96 original runs succeeded, so this dataset contains no observed failures from which to fit a failure classifier. The later research records include memory pressure and worker terminations, but a calibrated failure predictor and a beneficial deployed probing policy have not been demonstrated [7].
edits.reason: Tie the scope limitation directly to recorded evidence.

edits.before: On the 24 saved held-out rows, the LightGBM model has 13.84% MdAPE, compared with 23.01% for the family-median baseline. MdAPE is the median of absolute prediction error divided by actual runtime, multiplied by 100. It is not classification accuracy, and 100 - MdAPE is not a valid accuracy claim.
edits.after: The saved test set contains 24 rows from eight family/configuration groups. LightGBM achieved 13.84% median absolute percentage error (MdAPE), while the family-median baseline achieved 23.01% [7]. For each row, the absolute prediction error is divided by the measured runtime; MdAPE is the median of these percentages. It measures typical relative error on this test set. Subtracting it from 100 does not produce a classification-accuracy score.
edits.reason: Explain the result with its denominator and prevent an invalid accuracy interpretation.

edits.before: SAFE-Pipe demonstrates a reproducible, bounded configuration-advice workflow with an explicit predictor, upper runtime estimates, support checks, preference-based selection and abstention. The original dataset supports a small held-out runtime result and descriptive configuration comparisons. Later research shows why small execution probes can lose pressure information and cost more than they add on short jobs. The current evidence supports keeping the probe gate closed.
edits.after: The implemented advisor compares eight configurations within four fixed workload profiles. On the saved held-out rows, its runtime model obtained 13.84% MdAPE; fresh prospective validation remains pending. The later study found that quiet small probes could miss pressure seen at full input size, while the one-probe replay added cost without improving the stronger metadata-based choices. These findings support retaining the current metadata-based advice and keeping probe admission disabled for this use case [7].
edits.reason: Conclude with measured findings and the resulting design decision, within the tested scope.

edits.before: LightGBM predicts log successful engine runtime using 120 trees, seven leaves, learning rate 0.05, minimum child count three and L2 penalty one. Calibration uses the maximum log residual over each group’s repetitions. The nominal 90% finite-sample rank over 12 calibration groups selects the largest calibration score. The stored upper log offset is 0.523642, giving U = t * exp(0.523642), approximately 1.688 * t. The prediction and calibration components follow the methodological background in [4] and [5].
